query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

generation.hypothesis: The melting properties of high-melting refractory materials can be accurately calculated using the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT) with a machine learning-based interpolation scheme to reduce computational costs.
generation.material_initial_state: High-melting refractory materials in their solid state
generation.intervention: Application of the ab initio free-energy approach based on DFT with machine learning-based interpolation
generation.mechanism: Thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations with machine learning-based interpolation to reduce computational costs
generation.predicted_outcome: Accurate calculation of melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point
generation.boundary: Limitations of computational resources and accuracy of machine learning-based interpolation
generation.uncertainty: The accuracy of the machine learning-based interpolation scheme and the transferability of the model to different materials and conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of calculated melting properties with experimental measurements for a set of high-melting refractory materials
measurements: Volume change at the melting point
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the calculated melting properties deviate significantly from experimental measurements, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system. The requirements for designing novel metallic alloys that are capable of surpassing a whole set of specific properties of currently available commercial alloys are, at present, a subject of high demand in the industry. For instance, an improved combination of metallic alloys should possess strength and ductility while maintaining a relatively low cost. This is especially true when one is dealing with materials for high-temperature applications. Therefore, new engineering solutions are needed for novel materials that outperform the capabilities of the currently used Ni-based alloys. One of the prospective innovative materials that could be able to meet the requirements of such demanding applications, especially in the aviation and aerospace industries, may be refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). These are also known by other names, such as complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). These materials have been extensively studied in recent years [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] due to their very interesting combination of properties in some of the compositions.
